catalog_quote: In Khowar, word stress is lexically determined; that is, in each word a specific syllable is stressed. Stress has several functions in Khowar. First, it is lexically contrastive, indicating a meaning difference in several pairs of basic underived words; see examples in Table 2.10. Stress plays a morphological role in several contexts, for example in deriving nouns from adjectives, as in iskúrdi ‘short’ → iskurdí ‘shortness’. [...] Disyllabic nouns are stressed either on their final syllable: apák ‘mouth’, arqá ‘back’; or on their initial (in this case penultimate) syllable: áɫi ‘duck’, náqul ‘proverb’, ʋrázun ‘wing’. new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically assigned and contrastive (káɫi 'noodle soup' vs kaɫí 'yoke stick', béɫu 'basket' vs beɫú 'flute'); in uninflected words it falls on the final or the penultimate syllable (Liljegren & Khan 2017: final is the most frequent pattern, antepenult marginal at best). Certain suffixes are inherently stressed (oblique -ó, obl.pl -án, infinitive -ík, nominaliser -í, plural -gíni) and take the main stress when added (dust > dustó, iskúrdi > iskurdí), i.e. main stress goes to the rightmost lexically stressed morpheme; but stems with the lexical low-rising tone (lengthened vowel, e.g. doón 'ghee', braár 'brother') and a small set of kin terms (nan, tat, beč, mik) keep stress on the stem before -o/-an, and disyllables with final stress keep it (šapír-o). A marginal lexical low-rising tone (with vowel elongation) contrasts with default high-falling pitch on a small number of words (don 'tooth' vs doón 'ghee').
new_statements.secondary_stress: In compounds the primary stress of the first element is demoted to secondary stress (bašar̩.dóyu 'member of a funeral procession'); when a stressed suffix attaches to a polysyllable the earlier stress becomes secondary (noʋes-gíni). Strand 2012 likewise describes a secondary accent level in compounds/multi-word sequences on the normally accented vowel of a constituent. No rhythmic secondary stress described.
new_statements.exceptions: Low-tone (lengthened) monosyllabic stems and kin terms nan/tat/beč/mik/lu retain stem stress before oblique -o (nán-o, brár-o) whereas most monosyllables shift (dust-ó, šam-ó); žaʋ, ʋaʋ shift (žaʋ-ó); lu 'word' > lú-o is called an unexplained puzzle; enclitics like di 'also' unstressed; perfective participle stress placement varies; sentence/emphatic stress can override (γoš no boy-án).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical word stress in citation and inflected word forms; Bashir explicitly separates sentence stress (emphasis/focus shifts, utterance-final lengthening) from lexical stress. Description based on conservative Upper Chitral varieties (fieldwork 1986-2010); Liljegren & Khan's corroborating JIPA account is of Mastuj (Upper Chitral) speech, with acoustic note that pitch height/change is the main correlate of stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Both primary sources describe Upper Chitral Khowar: Bashir 2025 is based on fieldwork (1986-2010) with speakers of the conservative Upper Chitral varieties (Mulkhow/Torkhow/Mastuj area), Liljegren & Khan 2017 on the speech of Mastuj; both are Khowar proper = khow1242 (ISO khw). Bashir notes only minor dialect variation (Chitral Town, Swat Ushu/Mataltal, Ghizer/Gupis-Yasin in Gilgit-Baltistan); no separate glottocodes involved.

sources.note: 'Stress, tone and vowel duration' (pp. 224-227): 'The placement of stress is lexically contrastive in Khowar. The most frequent stress pattern is one with main stress on the final syllable, but it may also fall on the penultimate (and possibly even the antepenultimate) syllable of an uninflected word'; main correlate pitch, often with intensity; a minority of affixes lexically stressed, main stress on the rightmost lexically stressed syllable; separate lexical low(-rising) tone on some items which retains stress under affixation. Speech of Mastuj, Upper Chitral.

sources.note: Section 'Accent': 'The position of accent within words is distinctive. Accented phonation may occur on the penultimate or the final syllable in a simple, non-compounded word'; two accent types (anterior voicing = raised pitch, posterior voicing = lowered pitch); secondary accent in compounds/multi-word sequences on the normally accented vowel of a constituent.
